title: Miller Fisher Syndrome: The Neuro-Ophthalmic Triad
summary: A rare, acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy and a variant of Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS). It is clinically defined by the classic triad of ataxia, areflexia, and ophthalmoplegia, often triggered by molecular mimicry following a preceding infection.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Miller Fisher Syndrome (MFS) is an acute paralytic illness considered a regional variant of Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS). It is characterized by a unique tropism for the cranial nerves, particularly those governing ocular motility. The condition is strongly associated with anti-GQ1b IgG antibodies, which react with gangliosides concentrated at the nodes of Ranvier in oculomotor nerves and muscle spindles.

sections.title: Etiology & Pathophysiology
content: 1. Antecedent Infection: Campylobacter jejuni or Haemophilus influenzae.
2. Molecular Mimicry: Bacterial lipooligosaccharides resemble human gangliosides.
3. Antibody Production: Development of IgG anti-GQ1b antibodies.
4. Targeted Attack: Antibodies bind to high concentrations of GQ1b in CN III, IV, VI, and dorsal root ganglia.
5. Nerve Conduction Failure: Complement-mediated damage at the neuromuscular junction.

sections.title: Comprehensive Ocular Findings
content: Acute onset of bilateral symmetrical external ophthalmoplegia.
Diplopia is often the presenting complaint.
Ptosis (usually bilateral) is common.
Pupillary involvement (Internal Ophthalmoplegia) in 25-50% of cases.
Saccadic palsy or 'one-and-a-half' syndrome (rare).
Ocular bobbing or opsoclonus (rare reports).

sections.title: Extra-Ocular Clinical Features
content: Cerebellar-like ataxia: Disproportionate to the degree of sensory loss.
Generalized areflexia or marked hyporeflexia.
Bulbar palsy (dysarthria, dysphagia) in overlapping cases.
Mild distal sensory symptoms (paresthesias).
Facial nerve palsy (Bell's-like) in up to 30%.

content.mnemonic: Miller Fisher is a FAR-out Triad
content.explanation: F: Falls (Ataxia), A: Areflexia (Loss of reflexes), R: Red-reflex/Eyes (Ophthalmoplegia).

sections.title: Emergency Red Flags
content: Rapidly progressive respiratory distress (Diaphragmatic weakness).
Severe dysphagia (Aspiration risk).
Autonomic instability (Labile blood pressure, arrhythmias).
Decreased level of consciousness (Indicates Bickerstaff Encephalitis overlap).

rows: Diurnal fluctuation, no areflexia, no ataxia
MRI brain, clinical response to B1
Sudden onset, focal deficits, long-tract signs

sections.title: The Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. Serology: Anti-GQ1b IgG antibody (Highly sensitive: >90% in MFS).
2. Lumbar Puncture: Looking for Albuminocytologic Dissociation.
3. Neurophysiology: Nerve Conduction Studies (NCS) - showing reduced sensory nerve action potentials.
4. Neuroimaging: MRI Brain/Orbit to rule out structural/ischemic lesions.

rows: May be normal in the first week of symptoms

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocols
content: 1. Admission & Monitoring: Vital capacity, swallowing, and cardiac rhythm.
2. Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG): 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days.
3. Plasmapheresis (PE): 5 sessions over 1-2 weeks (alternative to IVIG).
4. Supportive Care: Lubricating drops for lagophthalmos, occlusion for diplopia.
5. Physical Therapy: Focus on balance and gait training.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Fellow
content: Anti-GQ1b antibodies are essentially 100% specific for this clinical spectrum.
Normal CSF in the first 48 hours does NOT rule out MFS.
The ataxia in MFS is peripheral (proprioceptive) rather than purely cerebellar.
Papilledema is rare but can occur due to high CSF protein levels.
If the patient is sleepy, look for Bickerstaff Brainstem Encephalitis overlap.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
sections.content: Recent research focuses on the 'GBS classification group' criteria which help distinguish MFS from other mimics earlier in the course. Landmark studies have shown that while IVIG hastens the onset of recovery, the ultimate long-term prognosis (at 6 months) is excellent regardless of treatment in mild cases, though treatment is standard of care to prevent progression to respiratory failure.
